purpose: Every shape Conduit invented where no ground truth existed, and the exact evidence that would displace it. This exists because the repository reversed a standing rule: it used to refuse a feature it could not ground, and now it builds one on an educated guess instead. That reversal is only safe if an invention stays distinguishable from a recovery for as long as it lives, and if the arrival of real evidence is an obligation to reimplement rather than an invitation to feel vindicated.
howThisIsEnforced: scripts/verify-conduit-inventions.mjs checks both directions: every CONDUIT-INVENTED marker in the source is registered here, and every entry here still exists in the source. A marker without a Displaced-by line fails. An entry whose displacement evidence has landed fails, which is the point -- the gate turns 'we should revisit this' into a build failure.

markerConvention.inSource: // CONDUIT-INVENTED: <id>\n// Displaced-by: <the capture or document that would settle it>
markerConvention.note: The id is <context>.<Symbol>. It is not a package path, so moving a file does not silently unregister an invention -- renaming the symbol does, which is when someone should be looking at this anyway.

displacementProcedure: When the named evidence lands, record it under docs/evidence/ or docs/apollo/ as a normal capture first. An invention displaced by nothing citable is just a different guess.

Reimplement against the evidence. Do not adapt the invented shape to fit -- the invented shape was chosen without constraint and will bend into agreement, which is how a guess becomes an unfalsifiable claim.
Delete the CONDUIT-INVENTED marker and this entry in the same change as the reimplementation, so the register never describes code that no longer exists.
State in the change what the invention got wrong. That is the only feedback anyone gets about how good these guesses are, and without it the next invention is made no better informed than this one.

inventions.what: Apollo-shaped resource identifiers for resources Apollo has published no type token for, minted under ri.conduit.main.<type>.<locator> rather than ri.apollo.
inventions.why: The grammar ri.<service>.main.<type>.<locator> is published, and the service segment names the service that owns the resource -- which is why Autopilot's teams are ri.autopilot and not ri.apollo. A Product that exists only in Conduit is owned by Conduit. Guessing a token inside ri.apollo instead would risk a silent collision: if Apollo's real token for something else matches the guess, two different objects share one identifier and nothing raises a hand. A Conduit-namespaced identifier can only be wrong in the direction of being obviously ours. ADR 0007 left this choice open and this is the answer.
inventions.displacedBy: A published statement giving Apollo's own type tokens for Product, Product Release or Bundle resource identifiers.
inventions.riskIfWrong: Low. The identifiers are opaque, self-consistent and unmistakably Conduit's, and every coordinate serving one discloses valueTier: CONDUIT_NATIVE. If Apollo's real tokens arrive, the values change but nothing was ever claimed to match them.

inventions.what: The locator segment of every Apollo resource identifier Conduit mints: the first 12 bytes of a SHA-256 over a stable input, hex encoded.
inventions.why: The grammar around it is published, not invented -- the pinned OpenAPI carries ri.apollo.main.environment.123, ri.apollo.main.installation.123 and ri.apollo.main.package.123, and ri.autopilot.main.team.123 shows the service segment naming the owning service. Only the locator is open, because Apollo's examples use the placeholder 123. A digest rather than a UUID because the value has to be stable across restarts and replicas without being stored; the one Apollo locator whose format is documented, a Plan's, is a UUID, so this is a known divergence rather than an unconstrained choice.
inventions.displacedBy: A published statement of Apollo's RID locator format, for any resource type Conduit holds.
inventions.riskIfWrong: Low in shape, moderate in consequence. The identifiers are opaque and self-consistent, so nothing inside Conduit breaks; but a client that round-trips one into a real Apollo API will not match anything, which is exactly why the coordinates serving them disclose valueTier: CONDUIT_NATIVE.

inventions.what: A per-recipient inbox record carrying its own read state.
inventions.why: Read state is modelled per-recipient because two people notified about the same promotion failure read it independently, and storing readAt on the event would let one of them mark it read for both. Apollo has an inbox -- Hub Settings carries a 'My notifications' page and the tenant viewer role names it -- but no capture shows an entry or its read state.
inventions.displacedBy: A capture of Apollo's notification inbox entry and its read state, in particular whether read state is per-recipient.
inventions.riskIfWrong: Medium. Wrong here means the inbox behaves differently from Apollo's, which is visible to operators but not corrupting.

inventions.what: Resolution of one event to its recipients, deduplicated per owner and channel.
inventions.why: Deduplication is a judgement, not a recovery: being told the same thing twice in the same place teaches people to ignore it. The channel half of the key is grounded -- Apollo configures email and in-app independently, so reaching one person on both is intended -- but collapsing one owner reached by two preferences on one channel is Conduit's own choice, and Apollo may well fan out per preference instead.
inventions.displacedBy: A capture of how Apollo resolves one event to its recipients, in particular whether it deduplicates a recipient reached by two preferences.
inventions.riskIfWrong: Low. Changing the fan-out rule changes delivery volume, not stored shape.

inventions.what: The rendered form of one inbox entry that a delivery transport sends: a subject line built from the event type and environment, a body of the emitter's summary followed by the event id, type, resource, environment, actor and time, and the destination the recipient's own contact resolved to, which is absent when they hold none.
inventions.why: Something has to decide the wording, and deciding it once in the domain is better than deciding it per adapter, where two transports would phrase the same failure differently and give an operator two facts to reconcile during an incident. Apollo's settings pages establish that email and Slack contacts receive notifications; no capture shows what the message looks like when it arrives, so every choice here -- that the subject leads with the type a subscriber filtered on, that the body repeats the identifiers needed to act without opening a console -- is Conduit's.
inventions.displacedBy: a capture of what Apollo puts in a notification email or Slack post, in particular whether the subject names the event type or the resource
inventions.riskIfWrong: Low and cosmetic in the near term: a wrong subject line is annoying rather than dangerous. It becomes expensive if anyone parses the body, because a downstream receiver built against this shape has to change when the real one arrives. That is why the webhook payload is versioned and structured rather than only textual.

inventions.what: The JSON body Conduit POSTs when delivering a notification to a configured webhook endpoint: a version discriminator, the event and recipient identity the delivery is keyed on, the rendered subject and body, a Slack-compatible text field, and an optional destination object naming the kind and address the recipient's own contact resolved to.
inventions.why: A transport had to exist for the readiness document's Tier 1 gap 1 to close, and a webhook is the one transport Conduit can honestly offer: SMTP needs a recipient address and no store in this repository holds one. Apollo establishes that a team may own a Slack contact and that Slack contacts are deliverable; nothing establishes the request Apollo makes, so the field names, the version discriminator and the decision to duplicate the body into a Slack-shaped text field are Conduit's own.
inventions.displacedBy: a capture of the request Apollo makes when it delivers to a Slack or email team contact, including its field names and headers
inventions.riskIfWrong: Moderate, because this one is on the wire. A receiver written against these field names has to change when the observed request arrives, and a deployment that has pointed a mail relay at this endpoint would keep delivering under the old shape until it did. The version discriminator exists so that change is detectable rather than silent.

inventions.what: The Hub's authenticated notification routes and their request and response shapes: GET /v1/notifications/inbox, GET /v1/notifications/events, GET and PUT /v1/notifications/preferences keyed on the (resource, owner, channel) tuple the store already holds one row for, and GET, PUT and DELETE /v1/notifications/contacts keyed on the (owner, kind) tuple the address book holds one row for.
inventions.why: The pinned Apollo OpenAPI under docs/apollo/snapshots/ publishes no notification operation -- the string does not occur in api-definition.yml -- so there was no published shape to be faithful to. The settings pages captured in docs/evidence/apollo-notification-types.json establish the grain being edited (a per-resource, per-channel preference list, For User or For Team) and nothing else about a wire format, so the routes carry that grain and invent only the spelling. Declining to build it was the alternative, and it leaves the Tier 1 readiness gap open: a preference editable only through the store is not editable.
inventions.displacedBy: A capture of Apollo's notification Hub API -- its route paths, its request and response shapes, and how it scopes an inbox read to a caller.
inventions.riskIfWrong: Low outside Conduit, moderate inside it. Nothing round-trips these shapes into Apollo, and the routes sit under /v1/notifications where no Apollo-shaped route lives, so a wrong guess cannot collide with a real operation. What a wrong guess costs is a console and any client written against it, which would have to be rewritten when the real shape arrives.

inventions.what: A stored destination per (owner, kind) -- an address, its kind, an opt-into-future-resources flag and its timestamps -- where the owner may be a TEAM or a USER, and an identifier minted as a digest over (owner, kind) rather than chosen or derived from the address.
inventions.why: Apollo establishes the team half: a contact is created in Hub Settings, has one of three kinds, is what a resource selects, and a team holding none receives nothing. It establishes no user contact at all, and may well have none -- a tenant's account email would do the same job. Conduit needs one anyway, because its preference model already admits a USER owner on the EMAIL channel and without an address that subscription reaches nobody, which is precisely the Tier 1 readiness gap this closes. Keying on (owner, kind) rather than on a contact identifier follows the dialog, which creates a contact of a kind for an owner; the identifier is derived from the same tuple so every replica mints it without storing it, and deliberately not from the address, because an identifier derived from an address carries the address wherever it travels and changes identity when somebody moves.
inventions.displacedBy: A capture of Apollo's contact API -- what a contact is keyed on, whether a user holds one at all, what it is called, and what its identifier looks like.
inventions.riskIfWrong: Moderate, and the highest-consequence entry in this register, because the value stored is personal data. Being wrong about the shape costs a migration. Being wrong about the authorization would cost somebody their mail, which is why the owner check admits no administrator override and is held down by TestThroughTheHubOnePrincipalCannotWriteAnotherPrincipalsContact rather than by this paragraph. A user contact that Apollo turns out not to have is a table Conduit stops writing, not a value anyone round-trips into Apollo.

inventions.what: The rule that turns one recipient into one destination at delivery time: skip contacts belonging to another owner, skip an in-app recipient entirely, skip any kind Apollo does not deliver to, prefer the kind whose name matches the channel, break remaining ties by kind name, and resolve to nothing when no contact qualifies -- which leaves the operator-configured endpoint as the fallback.
inventions.why: Something has to choose, because Apollo publishes two per-resource channels (EMAIL, IN_APP) and three contact kinds (EMAIL, SLACK, PAGERDUTY), and the two vocabularies overlap in exactly one place. What is grounded: PagerDuty receives nothing, so it is never a destination; an in-app entry is delivered by the inbox, so an address would send it somewhere its owner never chose. What is Conduit's: that a team whose only contact is Slack is reached there rather than not at all, that ties break by kind name so two replicas resolving at the same moment agree, and that a recipient with no contact falls back rather than failing. A failed read of the address book is deliberately not folded into 'no contact' -- that retries, because delivering to the fallback on a failed query would send a person's notification somewhere they did not choose.
inventions.displacedBy: A capture of how Apollo chooses which of a recipient's contacts a notification is delivered to, and what it does when the recipient has none.
inventions.riskIfWrong: Moderate. Wrong here changes where a notification lands rather than what is stored, and the fallback bounds the worst case at the behaviour that existed before contacts: a deployment that records no contacts is bit-for-bit unchanged. The direction that would cost most is preferring a kind Apollo would not have, which is why the kind is on the wire beside the address so a receiver can refuse one it does not expect.

inventions.what: Which of Apollo's two observed recall notification event types Conduit raises for a given recall: PRODUCT_IN_OPEN_ENDED_RECALL when the recall has no ending version and is not single-version, and PRODUCT_RECALLS otherwise.
inventions.why: Both labels are observed, in docs/evidence/apollo-notification-types.json, and so are their descriptions -- 'Future releases of this Product will be recalled' for the first, 'Anytime a bug or critical issue has been discovered in my product' for the second. A Conduit recall with no upper bound covers every version the Product will ever publish above its starting version, which is the first description exactly. What is not established is that Apollo distributes the two this way: the same capture records, as an upstream ambiguity, that nothing says whether these are two types or one type rendered at two granularities. Raising only one of them was the alternative, and it would have told a subscriber who ticked the other that no recall had opened.
inventions.displacedBy: a capture showing which notification event type Apollo raises for a recall with an ending version, against one without
inventions.riskIfWrong: Low, and reversible in one function. Nothing leaves Conduit under these type names except a notification a Conduit deployment delivers to its own configured transport, and both names are Apollo's own, so a wrong split mislabels an inbox row rather than inventing a vocabulary. What it costs is a subscriber who ticked exactly one of the two: they see the recalls Conduit routed to their type and not the others, which reads as no recall having opened.

displaced.whatTheInventionGotWrong: Its premise. The entry said Conduit 'carries the Environment where Apollo's documented example carries a Space'. Apollo's documented example carries no Space: the pinned OpenAPI publishes aeid:apollo-environment-demo:helm-chart:wordpress twice, beside environmentRid, and that second segment is an environment name. Conduit's aeid:<environment>:helm-chart:<entity> matches the published example in segment count, in the helm-chart product-type token, and in the meaning of the second segment. Nothing was invented; the construction was recovered and then filed as a guess.
displaced.howThisWentWrong: The grammar record's own conduitBearing already said the space-or-environment question was NOT established, and the invention entry -- written after reading it -- asserted it was a Space anyway. That is an inference hardening into a fact across two files in one day. The answer was in a snapshot this repository has held since the OpenAPI was pinned; nobody had compared the OSDK example against the OpenAPI example. The OSDK's 'mojito' says nothing about what it is, which is exactly why it should not have been read as saying 'Space'.
displaced.note: ApolloEntity.id still discloses valueTier: CONDUIT_NATIVE, and that is unchanged and correct: no Apollo Hub answered with the string, Conduit composed it from its own environment and entity names. Serving a value built to a published shape is still serving a value Conduit built.

displaced.whatTheInventionGotWrong: It existed at all. Apollo's notification subscriptions carry no severity: filtering is by type and channel, and nothing on any notification page or screenshot has a severity, priority or urgency control. The invention also named a displacement condition -- 'a capture establishing Apollo's MonitoringSeverity enum members' -- that could never have displaced it, because this repository's own reference note already records MonitoringSeverity as a Foundry Data Health type rather than an Apollo one. An invention whose stated evidence cannot settle it is unfalsifiable, which is the failure the register exists to prevent and which the register itself shipped.
displaced.note: Apollo does have a severity, on the Environment Events surface, where the 2020 capture shows the facet Success/Info/Warning/Error. That is a different surface and is not modelled here. Note also that the invented members -- INFO, WARNING, ACTION_REQUIRED, CRITICAL -- match neither that vocabulary nor its ordering.

displaced.whatTheInventionGotWrong: Every name, and worse, the shape. All eight invented kinds are gone; nine observed types replace them, and not one invented name survived. The structural error was closing the set: Apollo's documentation says the supported types 'will grow over time', and the settings page carries a per-resource, per-channel toggle reading 'If enabled, you will opt into future notification types added for this resource'. Apollo solved openness with forward consent. The invention closed the vocabulary and justified it by analogy to the Change Type taxonomy -- reasoning from a neighbouring design instead of looking, which is exactly how a closed set becomes the thing that silently drops every type added later.

The grain and three whole dimensions. Apollo's unit is a preference per (resource, principal, channel), not one subscription filtered by kind and severity. Missing entirely: delivery channels, team contacts as a prerequisite for a team receiving anything, and the two opt-into-future toggles. Present and wrong: a severity floor Apollo does not have, and a Muted boolean where Apollo's mute vocabulary belongs to monitors. The one part that held was ownership by user or team, which was the one part grounded in recovered evidence rather than guessed.

howThisWentWrong.note: All three displacements landed the day after the register was written, from evidence that was already in reach. This is recorded because the register's value depends on its guesses being honest ones, and these were not -- they were made without looking.
whatWasAvailable: Three public Palantir documentation pages under managing-notifications, already listed in docs/apollo/public-documentation-manifest.tsv with their content digests.

Five screenshots on those pages, already counted by docs/apollo/IMAGE-DERIVED-GAPS.md, which dispositioned the section 'Boundary' without opening them -- in a document whose own thesis is that screenshots are where a UI-first product states its enum values.
docs/ui/evidence/legacy-apollo-2020/environment-events.webp, committed in this repository, showing the Events severity and category facets.
howThisWentWrong.whyItWasNotSeen: docs/apollo/reference/notifications.md opened with 'No public Palantir docs page was captured for this capability'. That sentence was false against this repository's own manifest, had never been checked against it, and was taken at face value. The gate added in scripts/verify-documentation-claims.mjs now checks exactly this class of claim, because it is the cheapest possible check and nothing was doing it.
howThisWentWrong.lesson: The register asks whether an invention is marked and whether it names what would displace it. It does not ask whether the invention was necessary. A guess made without exhausting the sources already in the repository is not an educated guess, and marking it does not make it one.
